abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel conceptual framework that reconceptualizes context-aware systems through the lens of temporal dynamics and user attentional states. Traditional context-aware computing treats environmental conditions as static snapshots, failing to capture the inherently fluid nature of human activities and situational changes. We introduce the Dynamic Contextual Continuity Model (DCCM), which posits that effective ubiquitous computing requires systems to maintain coherent understanding of context transitions across time, accounting for cognitive load variations and attention fragmentation in modern multi-tasking environments. Through formal analysis using temporal logic and probabilistic state machines, we demonstrate how this paradigm shift enables more accurate prediction of user intentions and environmental evolutions. Our theoretical contributions include the formulation of context stability metrics and attention-aware adaptation policies that transcend conventional sensing-then-respond architectures. The proposed framework establishes new theoretical foundations for designing ubiquitous systems that perceive context not as discrete data points but as continuous experiential streams, fundamentally transforming how researchers approach context modeling in mobile computing and smart environment design.

Location-based services increasingly suffer from accuracy degradation in complex indoor environments where signal multipath effects and sensor noise compromise positioning reliability. This paper proposes an enhanced probabilistic framework for multi-sensor fusion that significantly improves indoor localization accuracy by explicitly modeling sensor dependency structures and environmental uncertainty correlations. Unlike existing approaches that treat sensor observations as conditionally independent, our method employs covariance-informed fusion with learned noise characteristics specific to different building structures and usage patterns. We formalize the theoretical bounds of positioning error under various environmental conditions and demonstrate that our approach achieves up to 34% improvement in localization accuracy compared to state-of-the-art Kalman filter-based methods across diverse test environments. The analytical framework provides designers with quantifiable guidance for sensor selection and placement optimization in pervasive computing deployments. Our contribution extends prior work by introducing adaptive noise modeling that dynamically adjusts to changing environmental conditions, offering a principled approach to building robust location-based services that maintain accuracy across varying user densities and infrastructure configurations.

We present AmbientFlow, a novel ambient intelligence system that fundamentally reimagines human-computer interaction through continuous implicit input interpretation embedded within smart environments. Unlike conventional wearable computing approaches that require explicit user engagement with devices, AmbientFlow leverages distributed room-scale sensing arrays to infer user intentions and emotional states from ambient behavioral cues, gait patterns, and physiological indicators captured through non-intrusive environmental sensors. The system architecture employs edge-computed neural networks for real-time inference, ensuring privacy preservation by processing sensitive biometric data locally rather than in the cloud. We implemented a complete prototype deployment across three diverse settings including a smart office, residential environment, and healthcare facility, conducting longitudinal studies with 87 participants over six months. The system demonstrates that ambient intelligence can achieve 89% accuracy in detecting user activity transitions and 82% accuracy in recognizing emotional states without any worn devices or explicit user input. This work establishes a new design paradigm for ubiquitous systems that shifts interaction from device-centric to environment-centric paradigms, fundamentally changing how users relate to computing infrastructure in their daily lives.

This paper introduces ContextLens, an improved context-aware mobile computing system that significantly advances the state-of-the-art in activity recognition through novel multi-modal sensor fusion and hierarchical classification architecture. Existing mobile activity recognition systems typically rely on shallow machine learning models operating on limited sensor modalities, resulting in suboptimal performance when users transition between activities or operate in environments with sensor interference. ContextLens addresses these limitations by integrating accelerometer, gyroscope, barometer, and Bluetooth beacon data through a novel attention-weighted fusion mechanism that dynamically adjusts sensor contributions based on environmental context and activity type. We developed an optimized mobile application that implements our approach with efficient on-device inference, achieving recognition accuracy of 94.2% across 12 activity categories while maintaining acceptable battery life through intelligent duty-cycling. Field evaluation with 52 participants across varied real-world scenarios demonstrates that our system outperforms existing approaches by 12-18% in accuracy, particularly excelling during activity transitions and in challenging conditions such as crowded spaces or variable lighting. The implementation provides actionable insights for developers seeking to build robust pervasive computing applications with improved user experience in mobile computing contexts.
